interest: This file provides significant insight into the high-stakes bureaucratic and logistical tensions between Washington and General Douglas MacArthur's occupation command over food allocations to post-war Japan. It highlights how the 1946 world food crisis forced U.S. policymakers to balance humanitarian and political stability requirements in occupied Japan against severe global grain deficits and domestic political resistance to rationing. The documents illuminate internal debates among top officials like Dean Acheson, William Clayton, Henry Wallace, and Clinton Anderson over controversial domestic interventions, such as corn price subsidies and wheat milling restrictions, as well as SCAP's evolving efforts through 1947 to compel Japanese farmers to meet food delivery quotas.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.6131, File 1588) covers matters related to Japanese agricultural production, grain collections, and food relief requirements under the Allied occupation from March 1946 to July 1947. It contains an internal State Department memorandum from March 1946 detailing Cabinet Subcommittee deliberations regarding General Douglas MacArthur's urgent request for 500,000 tons of grain shipments to Japan amid a severe global food shortage, the dispatch of an interdepartmental mission to Tokyo to assess food stocks and press for stricter indigenous collections, and proposed domestic U.S. conservation policies such as wheat milling curbs and corn subsidies. It also includes a July 1947 despatch from the U.S. Political Adviser for Japan in Tokyo transmitting Preliminary Study No. 13 of SCAP's Natural Resources Section, which analyzed the 1947 summer grain collection program and associated food administrative challenges in Japan.

subfiles.summary: The Office of the U.S. Political Adviser for Japan in Tokyo forwards to the Department of State copies of Preliminary Study No. 13, entitled '1947 Summer Grain Collection and Related Problems,' prepared by SCAP's Natural Resources Section on July 19, 1947. The report examines Japanese crop quotas, food distribution, and administrative obstacles to indigenous grain collection during the Allied occupation. A State Department Central Records (DC/R) replacement form is affixed to the front designating this copy as the official record copy.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1195 from Tokyo Transmitting Report on 1947 Summer Grain Collection

subfiles.about: Reports on a Cabinet Subcommittee meeting regarding General MacArthur's grain shipment requests for Japan, the global food crisis, and domestic grain conservation measures.
subfiles.from: James A. Stillwell (IR - Division of International Resources, Department of State)
subfiles.summary: James A. Stillwell reports to Under Secretary of State Dean Acheson on a meeting of the Cabinet Subcommittee called to consider General Douglas MacArthur's request for 500,000 tons of grain shipments to Japan for March 1946. Stillwell explains that total U.S. monthly shipments abroad cannot exceed 600,000 tons, making MacArthur's full request impossible to meet, and notes that a joint State-Agriculture mission headed by Colonel Harrison has flown to Japan to evaluate stocks and demand stricter domestic rationing. To maximize grain exports, Stillwell strongly recommends mandatory 25 percent milling restrictions on domestic wheat, a 25-cent per bushel corn subsidy to break black market withholding, and a presidential commitment to export over seven million tons of grain by the end of June.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from James A. Stillwell to Dean Acheson on Cabinet Subcommittee Meeting regarding Food Shipments to Japan
